facts.claim: Streaming credits list Dan Darmawan and David Burke (d4vd) as the writers and composers of "Romantic Homicide", released 20 July 2022 under D4VD ENT, LLC.
d4vd recorded the song on his phone in his younger sister's bedroom closet in Houston, Texas. It appears on the EP Petals to Thorns.
His usual process was to find a pre-made instrumental on YouTube, go into his sister's closet, and say whatever the instrumental needed him to say.
He told Songwriter Universe that he recorded the song straight off his phone and wrote it in about 30 minutes, in a flow state.
He worked on the song for a long time after a breakup without success. The breakthrough came in his bedroom closet, when he said "I'm scared", the song's opening line.
He had scrapped three earlier versions of the song before the released one.
In a Genius interview, d4vd said the "I killed you" lyric is figurative and happens in the mind, not literally.
d4vd said the song draws on Itami, the murderous alter ego of a detective character in a manga he was writing. Itami means "pain" in Japanese.
The song went viral on TikTok, entered the Billboard Hot 100 on the 17 September 2022 chart, and led to a Darkroom/Interscope record deal in August 2022.
d4vd (David Anthony Burke) began making music in late 2021 on the BandLab phone app after his Fortnite montage videos on YouTube got copyright strikes.

research.lineage: It sits in the bedroom-pop and TikTok-era, phone-recorded DIY tradition, with moody indie-rock and alt-R&B leanings.

draft:
**Romantic Homicide** opens with two words most breakup songs spend three minutes avoiding: "I'm scared." No setup, no scene, just the admission. d4vd has said that line was the breakthrough. He had worked on the song for a long time after a breakup without getting anywhere, scrapped three earlier versions, and then, sitting in his younger sister's bedroom closet in Houston, said it out loud. The rest came in about 30 minutes, in what he called a flow state, recorded straight onto his phone.

That order matters, because the song is built on fear wearing a disguise. The early lines are almost polite. He asks to be enlightened and wonders why he's still here, the voice of someone holding on long after being let go. Then the waiting curdles. Tired of standing by for someone who won't arrive, he does the one thing that ends waiting: he imagines the other person gone. The killing happens "in the back of my mind," and d4vd has been clear that it is figurative, a death that stays in the head. He doesn't cry. He doesn't regret it. The numbness is the point. Not grieving is a way of taking the power back.

What keeps the song from being a pose is the flinch that follows: "I can't believe I said it." For one line, the narrator hears himself and is startled. Then he doubles down, "But it's true," and the last words land flat and final: "I hate you." Shame and defiance sit right next to each other, and neither wins. d4vd has said the song draws on Itami, the murderous alter ego of a detective in a manga he was writing. Itami means "pain" in Japanese, which is a neat key to the whole thing: the killer here is hurt, given a name and a voice.

The music doesn't dramatize any of it. A clean electric guitar turns over an arpeggiated chord pattern, the bass holds simple sustained root notes, and the drums keep a steady, driving beat at a moderate tempo. The voice is clear and a little nasal, melodic and sustained, with no harmonies to soften it. That evenness is what makes the lyric chilling. He describes a death in his head the way you'd describe weather.

It's a bedroom-pop record in the most literal sense, one of the phone-made, TikTok-carried songs of its moment, with a moody indie-rock frame and some alt-R&B in the phrasing. It went viral, reached the Billboard Hot 100, and led to a Darkroom/Interscope deal. Credits list Dan Darmawan and David Burke as writers.

The song lets you say the ugliest thing heartbreak makes you think, then catch yourself saying it, and that small gasp of recognition is what keeps pulling you back.
